Six sites and six means is a table you can read by eye. Most groupings are not six.

This session takes the sentence you just learned and puts it under load. You will ask for
several summaries in one call instead of one, ask for different summaries of different columns,
rank a grouped result the way you ranked a raw table on Wednesday, and meet what happens when
you group by two things at once.

The data is one you have already interrogated: the National Park Service visitor records from
Wednesday's colab. You ranked individual park-years then. Today you rank parks.

By the end of this session you will be able to:

- pass a **list** to `.agg()` to get several summaries of one column
- pass a **dictionary** to `.agg()` to summarise several columns differently
- apply the **top-N sentence** to a grouped result
- recognize a **MultiIndex** produced by grouping on two keys, and flatten it with
  `.reset_index()`
- say why a grouped mean without a count next to it is a number you should not publish

[Session Webpage](https://eds-217-essential-python.github.io/course-materials/interactive-sessions/5b_aggregating_data.html)

4. Read the visitor records and rebuild the two subsets you made on Wednesday: the rows that
   describe a real year, and the rows that describe a National Park.

```{python}
import pandas as pd

url = 'https://eds-217-essential-python.github.io/data/national_parks.csv'
parks = pd.read_csv(url)

by_year = parks[~(parks['year'] == 'Total')].copy()
national_parks = by_year[by_year['unit_type'] == 'National Park'].copy()

national_parks.shape
```

4,682 rows. Each one is a single park in a single year, running from 1904 to 2016, and there are
61 distinct parks in there.

## One column, several summaries

Start with what you already know how to write:

```{python}
national_parks.groupby('region')['visitors'].mean()
```

Seven regions, seven means. And now the question that should be a reflex by the end of today:
how many rows went into each of those?

```{python}
national_parks.groupby('region')['visitors'].count()
```

Two calls, two Series, and you are already reading across them by eye and hoping you have lined
them up correctly. `.agg()` fixes that. Give it a **list** of aggregation names and it runs all
of them on the same grouping and puts the answers side by side:

```{python}
national_parks.groupby('region')['visitors'].agg(['count', 'mean', 'max'])
```

That is a DataFrame, not a Series. One row per group, one column per thing you asked for, and
the group labels are the index.

The names in the list are strings, and they are the same names you would have called as methods:
`'count'`, `'mean'`, `'sum'`, `'min'`, `'max'`, `'median'`, `'std'`, `'nunique'`.

:::{.callout-note}
🐍 `.agg(['mean'])` with one name in the list gives you a DataFrame with one column. `.mean()`
gives you a Series. Same numbers, different shape. Ask for the shape you want to work with next.
:::

## The reason `count` goes first

Look at that table again. `NE` has the highest mean of any region by a wide margin, more than
1.6 million visitors. If you were writing a report about which region of the park system draws
the crowds, `NE` is your headline.

Now read the `count` column. `NE` has 179 rows out of 4,682. Ask how many *parks* that is:

```{python}
national_parks.groupby('region')['unit_name'].nunique()
```

Two. The entire Northeast region contains two national parks, Acadia and Shenandoah, and both of
them are unusually busy. The mean is not wrong. It is just not a statement about a region, it is
a statement about two parks that happen to share a region code.

`NC` is worse: one park, 46 rows, and a mean printed to the same number of decimal places as a
mean computed from 1,590.

:::{.callout-important title="A mean is a summary of a count you did not print"}
Every grouped mean is really two numbers, and pandas shows you one of them. The habit that will
save you the most public embarrassment in your career is small: **put `'count'` first in every
`.agg()` list you write**, and read it before you read anything else.
:::

:::{.callout-tip title="✏️ Test your knowledge"}
Group `national_parks` by `state` and use `.agg()` with a list to get the count, mean and max of
`visitors`. Find a state whose mean looks impressive and whose count says you should not be
impressed. Name it, and say in one sentence what you would report instead.
:::

## Several columns, summarised differently

The list form runs the same summaries on one column. Often you want something else: the mean of
this column, the sum of that one, the number of distinct values in a third.

For that, `.agg()` takes a **dictionary**. The keys are column names and the values are what to
do with each:

```{python}
national_parks.groupby('region').agg({
    'visitors': 'mean',
    'unit_name': 'nunique',
    'year': 'min'
})
```

Read that as three separate instructions applied to the same split: average the visitors, count
the distinct park names, and find the earliest year of record.

Two things changed from the list form, and both follow from what a dictionary is:

- there is **no `['column']`** before `.agg()`. The keys of the dictionary say which columns, so
  naming a column beforehand would be saying it twice.
- the result has **one column per key**, named after the key.

This is the same dictionary you have been writing since Day 2. You used one to rename columns in
`.rename(columns={...})`. Same syntax, same idea: a mapping from a name to what should happen to
it.

:::{.callout-note}
🐍 A dictionary value can also be a **list**, which combines both forms:

```{python}
national_parks.groupby('region').agg({
    'visitors': ['count', 'mean'],
    'unit_name': 'nunique'
})
```

The column headings stack into two rows when you do this, which is a shape that gets awkward
fast. It is worth being able to read. Reach for it sparingly.
:::

:::{.callout-tip title="✏️ Test your knowledge"}
Write one `.agg()` call, grouped by `region`, that reports the **median** number of visitors,
the **latest** year of record, and the number of distinct **states** in each region. Then say in
one sentence why the median might be the more honest of the two averages for this data.
:::

## Ranking a grouped result

On Wednesday afternoon you learned the top-N sentence:

```python
df.sort_values('column', ascending=False).head(n)
```

You wrote it against raw tables. A grouped result is a table too, so the sentence works there
without modification, and the combination answers a question the raw table could not.

Wednesday's ranking found the single busiest **park-year**. This finds the busiest **park**:

```{python}
national_parks.groupby('unit_name')['visitors'].mean().sort_values(ascending=False).head(10)
```

Read that left to right and it is four instructions, two from today and two from Wednesday:
group by park, average the visitors, put the averages in order, take the front.

Great Smoky Mountains averages nearly three times the Grand Canyon over its record, which is not
what most people would guess. It is free to enter and it straddles a major road, and it has been
the busiest unit in the system for most of a century.

The same sentence run the other way gives the quietest parks:

```{python}
national_parks.groupby('unit_name')['visitors'].mean().sort_values().head(5)
```

When the grouped result is a DataFrame rather than a Series, `.sort_values()` needs to be told
which column to sort on, exactly as it does on a raw table:

```{python}
park_stats = national_parks.groupby('unit_name')['visitors'].agg(['count', 'mean', 'max'])

park_stats.sort_values('mean', ascending=False).head(10)
```

Now the count is right there next to the mean while you read the ranking, which is the whole
argument of the previous section arriving as a habit instead of a warning.

:::{.callout-caution title="Averaging across unequal records"}
`count` in that table is the number of **years** each park has been reporting, and it ranges
from 13 to over 100. Cuyahoga Valley's average is computed from 39 years, all of them recent.
Yellowstone's is computed from 113, most of them before mass car ownership.

Ranking parks by their all-time average is therefore partly a ranking of *when each park
existed*. This is not a flaw in your code. It is a question you have to answer before your
ranking means anything, and the honest fix is usually to filter to a common set of years first,
then group.
:::

:::{.callout-tip title="✏️ Test your knowledge"}
Filter `national_parks` to the single year `'2016'`, then group by `state` and use `.agg()` to
report the count and mean of `visitors`. Rank the result by mean. Compare your top three with
the all-time ranking above. Did anything move? Say in one sentence which of the two rankings you
would put in front of a park superintendent, and why.
:::

## Grouping by two keys

Everything so far has split the table by one column. `.groupby()` will take a **list** of
columns and split by all of them together, making one group per combination that actually
occurs:

```{python}
national_parks.groupby(['region', 'state'])['visitors'].mean()
```

Twenty-eight groups, because most states hold parks in only one region. Look at the left-hand
side of that output: there are two levels of labels, and the outer one is not repeated on every
row. That is a **MultiIndex**, an index made of more than one column.

A MultiIndex is genuinely useful and it is also the single most common reason a beginner's
pandas code stops working, because everything you know about selecting from an index now needs a
tuple:

```{python}
two_key = national_parks.groupby(['region', 'state'])['visitors'].mean()

two_key['IM', 'WY']
```

You are not expected to become fluent in this. You are expected to **recognize it and get out of
it**, and the way out is one method:

```{python}
flat = two_key.reset_index()
flat.head()
```

`.reset_index()` takes the index levels and turns them back into ordinary columns. What comes
back is a plain DataFrame with three columns, and every single thing you have learned this week
works on it again:

```{python}
flat.sort_values('visitors', ascending=False).head(5)
```

```{python}
flat[flat['region'] == 'PW'].sort_values('visitors', ascending=False)
```

:::{.callout-tip title="🧭 When to reach for `.reset_index()`"}
Whenever a grouped result is going to be **used** rather than **read**. If you are filtering it,
merging it, plotting it, or writing it to a file, flatten it first. If you are looking at it in
a notebook cell and moving on, leave it alone.

`.reset_index()` also works on a single-key grouped result, and turns the Series into a
two-column DataFrame. That is often exactly what you want before plotting.
:::

:::{.callout-tip title="✏️ Test your knowledge"}
Run `national_parks.groupby(['region', 'unit_name'])['visitors'].agg(['count', 'mean'])` and
look at the shape of what comes back. Then call `.reset_index()` on it and use the top-N
sentence to find the five busiest parks. Say in one sentence what `.reset_index()` changed.
:::

## Putting it together

One question, answered properly, using every piece of today so far:

> Which national parks in the Pacific West region have drawn the most visitors, and how much
> record is each average built on?

```{python}
pacific_west = national_parks[national_parks['region'] == 'PW']

pw_stats = pacific_west.groupby('unit_name')['visitors'].agg(['count', 'mean', 'max'])

pw_stats.sort_values('mean', ascending=False).head(10)
```

Filter, group, aggregate, rank. Four sentences, three of them learned earlier this week, and the
answer is a table you would be willing to defend.

## Key points

- `.agg(['count', 'mean', 'max'])` runs **several summaries on one column** and returns a
  DataFrame.
- `.agg({'col': 'fn', 'other': 'fn'})` runs **different summaries on different columns**. There
  is no `['column']` before it, because the dictionary keys name the columns.
- Put `'count'` first, every time. A grouped mean without a count beside it is half a number.
- The **top-N sentence** works on a grouped result: `.groupby(...)...sort_values(...).head(n)`.
- On a grouped DataFrame, `.sort_values()` needs the name of the column to sort by.
- Grouping by a **list** of keys produces a **MultiIndex**.
- `.reset_index()` turns index levels back into columns. Use it whenever the result is going to
  be used rather than just read.
